In the Bahá'í writings, justice is held to be the very foundation of human order and affection. Shoghi Effendi records that justice is extols as [“the light of men” and their “guardian”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, upon which [“the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) depend — *God Passes By*. 

Beyond this grand scale, justice is also a deeply personal moral compass. Howard Colby Ives points to Bahá’u’lláh's definition that invites each person to look inward: [“Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself,”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*. 

Earl Redman notes that in the *Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh writes simply that [“Justice is to be loved above all.”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*. It is a standard meant to bridge East and West, giving all souls an equal place.

Dear friend,

It is a quiet joy to look into this with you. What a wonderful question to carry, and what striking paths the writings open when we follow them. 

When we look to what the Bahá'í writings say about justice, we find it described not merely as a legal mechanism or a set of rules, but as something living, luminous, and foundational to human life. In *God Passes By*, Shoghi Effendi records that [Justice He extols as “the light of men” and their “guardian,” as “the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — affirming that upon it must depend ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind."](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) He also points to its two pillars, ["reward and punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-elfendi?paraId=para_510), characterizing them as the sources of life to the human race.

Beyond its cosmic and social organization, justice is also brought very close to the daily life of the individual conscience. In *Portals to Freedom*, Howard Colby Ives reflects on a definition from Bahá'u’lláh: 

> "Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself,"

It makes one pause, doesn't it? When we test our own sense of justice against that measure, it asks us to step entirely outside of our personal reactions and self-interest. 

There is also a very practical side to how justice is understood and applied among people. In *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*, Bahá’u’lláh addresses the criterion of justness in testimony, noting that ["The criterion of justness is a good reputation among the people. The testimony of all God’s servants, of whatever faith or creed, is acceptable before His Throne."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=para_356) And in Earl Redman's *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*, we are reminded of a simple, beautiful imperative from the Hidden Words: ["Justice is to be loved above all."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116)

I hope these fragments give you much to ponder as you read and walk your path. Please let me know where your curiosity leads you next.

Warmly,
Anís

That is a very real weight to carry, and it is a question many ask when they look at how human laws are made and enforced. 

Looking at the traditions themselves, justice is not described as the mere decree of the powerful, but as something rooted beyond human rulers. In the Qur'an, justice belongs to a higher authority, asking, ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*. The text contrasts human decrees with divine order, asking, ["Desire they, therefore, the judgments of the *times of* ignorance?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_rodwell-tr?paraId=para_444) — *The Qur'an (Rodwell)*. Similarly, in the Gathas, righteousness is a primal choice of the bounteous spirit who ["chose the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas*. 

At the same time, human power can certainly corrupt practice. Buddhist texts note how worldly power shifts depending on status, such as when ["a goat butcher is empowered to beat or bind or slay"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-l?paraId=para_1064) a poor person differently than another — *Sutra Collection (L)*. The traditions distinguish between ideal divine justice and flawed human application.

That view has a long history, and it is held by many thoughtful people: that external laws and the enforcement of the state are what actually hold society together, while religion is secondary. 

Yet some traditions see the causation running the other way. In *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*, Shoghi Effendi quotes Bahá’u’lláh describing religion as ["the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world and for the peaceful contentment of all that dwell therein"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. From this perspective, when the inner restraint of religion weakens, the rule of force and external laws must step in, but they can never fully replace it. 

Similarly, in the *Tao Te Ching*, Lao-tzu suggests that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279) — *Tao Te Ching*, implying that mere legal control cannot create true social harmony.

That is a natural place to look for order, and it is a path many societies have tried by building prisons and punishing crime to ["reform the criminal"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — *Some Answered Questions*. 

Yet the texts suggest that outward force cannot reach the root of the matter. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá warns that a system relying on punishment and chains ["only brings about the degradation of morals and the subversion of character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — *Some Answered Questions*. Instead of closing every door to wrong through coercion, the true work is to ["ensure that souls are properly educated"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — *Some Answered Questions* so they acquire virtues freely. Confucius similarly looks to the influence of good people who can ["do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553) — *The Analects* through moral power rather than fear. 

When a choice for good is forced upon us, it leaves no room for character to grow. What do you think happens to our sense of right and wrong when we only avoid evil because of a penalty?

That heavy feeling of falling short is something even the teachers of the past knew well. Confucius spoke of the weight upon his mind of ["inability to walk according to knowledge received"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) — *The Analects*. 

The point of trying is simply the turning toward what is right, again and again, even when plans unravel and the effort feels broken. As Vyasa counsels in the *Mahabharata*, the call is to ["practise righteousness"](https://siftersearch.com/library/hindu/mahabharata-12_vyasa#p1768) and remain ["firmly devoted to righteousness"](https://siftersearch.com/library/hindu/mahabharata-12_vyasa#p1768) — *The Mahabharata 12*. The striving itself is the path, not a test you pass or fail once and for all.

You’ve noticed a striking resemblance in how both traditions describe divine guidance entering the world. 

There is truth in what you see: in Hindu thought, avatars are described as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57) — *The Mahabharata 6*, while in the Bahá'í writings, the Manifestations are described as ["essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán*. 

Yet it seems to me that looking beneath the surface reveals a difference in how they appear. Hindu avatars, within the epic literature, often descend in specific physical forms to restore order when dharma declines. The Bahá'í writings speak of Manifestations as "Well-springs of divine knowledge" whose differing words stem from ["this difference in their station and mission"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) rather than distinct bodily descents. 

Outwardly similar ideas can carry entirely different architectures of meaning. Which of the two traditions would you be most interested in exploring next?

You are entirely right to notice how broadly the Bahá’í teachings speak about the world's spiritual traditions, drawing them together under one canopy. 

There's something important the writings add, though, which is that while they are seen as coming from one divine source, they are not viewed as identical in their social laws or specific details. Shoghi Effendi writes that the Faith has ["assimilated, by virtue of its creative, its regulative and ennobling energies, the varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. 

I read this as a unity of origin and purpose rather than a sameness of every teaching. The essential spiritual truths are seen as unfolding progressively over time, meeting the changing needs of humanity, even as the specific social laws of each revelation differ from age to age.

It is completely understandable to wonder about this, especially when so much of what we hear on the subject comes from the talks and writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá. 

However, the records of the tradition point elsewhere. In *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*, David Hofman writes that ["the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) is among ["the humanitarian principles which are explicit in His teaching"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) (*George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*). Similarly, Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab records 'Abdu'l-Bahá explaining that ["in the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to shoulder"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) (*'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt'*), and that ["the same education must be given to women as to men"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-bahas-second-visit-to-britain#p1054) because ["For His Holiness Bahá’u’lláh hath willed it so"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) (*'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt'* and *Abdu'l-Bahá's Second Visit to Britain*).

It is a wonderful thing to be moved by. There is a lovely line in Gladys Weeden's notes where she writes that ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*. 

If you enjoy how different texts trace this shared root, you might also like how Yusuf Ali translates the remembrance that ["Mankind was but one nation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1579) — *The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*. It is a quiet thought to carry with you: that our very differences unfolded upon a ground that was once undivided.

You are entirely right to see a connection between the two, as they belong together in the same tradition, but they are distinct books. 

Shoghi Effendi explains that the Kitáb-i-Aqdas is a later, mightier revelation that was ["Alluded to in the Kitáb-i-Íqán"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By*. 

The Kitáb-i-Íqán (the Book of Certitude) came first, laying spiritual foundations, while the Kitáb-i-Aqdas (the Most Holy Book) followed as the principal repository of law.

I am so sorry for the loss of your father. 

When looking into what the writings say about the soul after death, the Hindu tradition describes different paths depending on a person's inner state. Vyāsa writes in *The Bhagavad-Gita* that a soul ["fixed in Soothfastness, it goeth to the place"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) of those who know the truth, while a soul departing in "hardened Ignorance" is born anew. 

Other traditions record questions about these movements after death, as when disciples asked the Buddha ["What are his movements after death?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) in the *Sutra Collection*.

That is an ancient and lovely question. 

Ethel Stephana Stevens records asking it directly to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, noting that ["prayer was necessary, since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) — *Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*. The texts remind us that ["Every single thing is before His sight"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1950) — *The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*. 

Yet prayer remains advocated for soul growth, leaving every person ["responsible for his own soul growth"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) — *Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*. It seems to me that prayer changes the one who prays, turning the heart toward what it already receives. 

What draws you to ask about this today?

It is completely natural to feel protective of Christ's unique standing. 

The record from pilgrim notes indicates that Bahá'u'lláh and the Báb ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California* — and offered Christ ["such a praise, beyond the description and imagination"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. The text also states that Bahá'u'lláh wrote ["many commentaries on the Gospel, bringing to light its inner significances"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. 

Whether that reverence matches a Christian understanding is a different question, but the sources presented here do show a deep honor given to Him. You might enjoy looking into those Gospel commentaries yourself to see how His words are read there, whenever you feel inclined.

I can't find anything about Jesus in the texts I am able to search here. The passages mention alms, orphans, the early community of emigrants, the life and miracles of the Prophet, and the prayers of Adam, but they do not touch upon Jesus. 

If you would like to explore further, perhaps you might find what you are looking for by searching within a collection specifically dedicated to the Qur'an's chapters that recount his birth and ministry, such as *Surah Maryam* (Chapter 19) or *Surah Al-Imran* (Chapter 3).

I must be completely honest with you: looking through the texts available to me here, I couldn't find anything that describes compassion. 

The passages I can search do touch on other vital teachings, such as how a monk guards the senses so that ["evil, unskillful qualities such as greed or distress might assail him"](https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/dn/dn.11.0.than.html) — *Digha Nikaya 11 - Kevaddha Sutta (To Kevaddha)*, and how ["the Buddha actually opens"](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35895) the door of immortality through the continuity of one's deeds rather than an ego-entity (*The Gospel of Buddha*). But they do not speak directly to the definition or description of compassion. 

If you have a particular discourse or text in mind where compassion is discussed, please let me know, and I would be glad to look at it with you.

Yes, a scientist can certainly hold faith. The texts we have suggest that inquiry and belief need not stand at odds. 

In the Bahá'í tradition, Doris McKay records the perspective that ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*, asking, "How can one truth contradict another truth?" Similarly, Buddhist commentary notes that ["A scientific world such as todays will be able to accept gladly all ten tenets"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) of the *Kalama Sutta* — *Sutra Collection (HIJK)*, finding that true scientific standards emphasize verification in a way that aligns with the tradition's approach to testing truth. 

Doubt is a natural part of weighing evidence, and it deserves patience. When you look at how different traditions view the intellect, they often welcome careful questioning rather than fear it.

I couldn't find anything on quantum computing in the texts I can search. 

The writings do record Bahá’u’lláh speaking of a divine Force whose ["vibrating influence"](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99) has ["upset the equilibrium of the world and revolutionized its ordered life"](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-divine-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99) (*The Advent of Divine Justice*), and a scholar notes that He affirmed He would ["raise up scientists of great calibre who will bring about such marvellous technological achievements that no one can as yet imagine them"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) (*The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3*), but quantum computing itself is not mentioned.
